nameStory: The name "tearthumb" comes from the tiny, sharp prickles that run backward along the stems and leaf edges - they'll catch and tear at your thumb (and fingers) if you're not careful! The "arrow-leaved" part refers to the distinctive arrowhead shape of the leaves, which is actually quite unusual in the smartweed family.
description: Arrow-leaved tearthumb is a climbing annual plant that can scramble up to 6 feet tall using its prickly stems to grab onto other vegetation. It has distinctive arrowhead-shaped leaves that set it apart from its smartweed relatives, and produces small clusters of white to pink flowers. The entire plant is armed with tiny backward-pointing prickles that make it quite "grabby" to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive arrowhead or heart-shaped leaves up to 4 inches long with sharp-pointed tips and backward-pointing lobes at the base, feeling smooth except for tiny prickles along the edges

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Green, ribbed stems covered with small, sharp, backward-pointing prickles that catch on clothing and skin - run your finger down the stem and it feels smooth, but up the stem it's rough and grabby

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale pink flowers clustered in round to oval heads about half an inch long, appearing from midsummer through fall

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbing or sprawling vine-like plant that uses its prickles to scramble over and through other vegetation, often forming tangled masses

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, three-sided seeds enclosed in papery coverings that often persist into winter

habitat: Look for arrow-leaved tearthumb in wet areas like stream banks, pond edges, marshes, and ditches throughout New England. It thrives in moist soils and often grows alongside cattails, jewelweed, and other wetland plants. You'll also find it in wet meadows and the soggy edges of wooded swamps.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring with their characteristic arrow-shaped leaves already visible, though they're still small and not yet climbing.
seasonality.summer: Plants rapidly grow and climb through midsummer, with flower clusters appearing in July and August - this is the best time for identification when both leaves and flowers are present.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming into early fall, followed by dark seeds that ripen in September and October, while the prickly stems become more noticeable as other vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried seed clusters, but the annual plant has died - look for the three-sided seeds scattered on the ground or caught in dried vegetation.

funFact: Despite its grabby nature, arrow-leaved tearthumb is actually an important food plant - the seeds are eaten by numerous waterfowl and songbirds, and the young leaves are edible for humans when cooked (though harvesting them without getting scratched is quite the challenge!).
confusionNotes: The arrow-shaped leaves make this plant pretty distinctive, but it's sometimes confused with halberd-leaved tearthumb, which has more triangular leaves with outward-pointing side lobes (like a medieval halberd weapon) rather than backward-pointing ones. Memory trick: arrow-leaved has lobes that point backward like arrow fletching, while halberd-leaved has lobes that stick out to the sides.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name recently changed from Polygonum sagittata to Persicaria sagittata, so you might see it listed under either name in older field guides. Many people still call the whole group "polygonums" informally, even though botanists have split them into separate genera.
compareHints: Among its smartweed relatives, arrow-leaved tearthumb is unique for its arrowhead-shaped leaves - most other Persicaria species have lance-shaped or oval leaves. It's also more climbing and vine-like than most smartweeds, and along with halberd-leaved tearthumb, it's one of the only two "tearthumbs" with those distinctive backward-pointing prickles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many smartweeds, low smartweed stands out for its distinctly bristly leaf sheaths and sprawling, ground-hugging habit - most other smartweeds grow more upright.

American jumpseed is unique among New England's Persicaria species for its woodland habitat preference - nearly all its relatives prefer sunny, wet areas like marshes, pond edges, or disturbed ground.

Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, halberd-leaved tearthumb is unique for its climbing habit and distinctive leaf shape - most other smartweeds and knotweeds are upright plants with oval or lance-shaped leaves.
Far Eastern smartweed differs from spotted lady's thumb by having longer, more cylindrical flower clusters rather than short oval ones.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, water smartweed is unique in its amphibious lifestyle and dramatically different leaf forms.
Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, spotted lady's thumb is one of the easiest to identify thanks to its distinctive dark leaf spots - most other smartweeds lack this feature.

Mile-a-minute differs from its native relatives like arrow-leaved tearthumb and halberd-leaved tearthumb primarily in leaf shape - it has equilateral triangular leaves while the others have arrow or halberd-shaped leaves with distinct pointed lobes.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, pinkweed stands out with its particularly dense, cylindrical flower clusters and robust growth habit.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, pale smartweed stands out for its consistently pale flowers - most other smartweeds have brighter pink blooms.
Among New England's many smartweeds, swamp smartweed stands out for its mild taste and preference for the wettest spots.
Among the many Persicaria species in New England, Asian jumpseed stands out for its delicate, thin growth habit and light green leaves with brown spots.
Among its many smartweed relatives, dotted smartweed is distinguished by those translucent leaf dots and its preference for very wet conditions.
Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, waterpepper stands out for its intensely peppery taste and drooping flower spikes.
Among the many Persicaria species in New England, Nepal persicaria is distinguished by its relatively recent arrival and limited distribution.
Puritan Smartweed differs from other New England smartweeds by its preference for sandy rather than muddy habitats and its extremely limited distribution.

Among its knotweed relatives, kiss-me-over-the-garden-gate stands out dramatically with its large size and distinctive drooping flower spikes - most other Persicaria species have much smaller, upright flower clusters.
Carey's Smartweed differs from its common cousin spotted lady's thumb by having much sparser, more open flower clusters and lacking the dark triangular spots on the leaves.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, small water-pepper stands out for its truly diminutive size and exceptionally short flower clusters.
Among New England's smartweeds, bog smartweed's thread-like leaves are diagnostic – no other Persicaria species has such narrow foliage.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, Asian lady's thumb stands out for its low, mat-forming growth habit rather than the upright stance of most smartweeds.
Among New England's many smartweeds, stout smartweed lives up to its name with the thickest, most substantial stems in the genus.

Among New England's many Persicaria species, dense-flowered smartweed stands out for its exceptionally compact, bottlebrush-like flower spikes - much denser than the looser clusters of spotted lady's thumb or pinkweed.

Among New England's many Persicaria species, Japanese indigo is most similar to spotted lady's thumb and pinkweed in overall appearance, but it's much rarer and has a more upright, less sprawling growth habit.
